exercises.name: Barbell Bench Press
exercises.biomechanics: Trains horizontal shoulder adduction and elbow extension, overloading the chest in the mid-to-short range.
setup_cues: Lie flat on the bench with eyes directly under the bar.
Set a firm grip slightly wider than shoulder width.
Keep feet flat on the floor and pull shoulder blades back and down.
Unrack the bar and stabilize it directly over the chest.
common_mistakes: Flaring elbows out to 90 degrees, stressing the shoulder joint.
Bouncing the bar off the chest.
Lifting feet or hips off the bench during the lift.
exercises.progression: Increase weight slowly while keeping 1-3 reps in reserve; use a spotter when lifting near failure.
exercises.regression: Dumbbell bench press or push-ups to practice chest recruitment with lighter loading.

expert_rating.verdict: Great strength benchmark, but chest stretch is limited by the physical bar hitting the chest.

exercises.plain_summary: The classic chest builder: press a bar off your chest to load your pecs, front delts, and triceps together.

exercises.name: Dumbbell Bench Press
exercises.biomechanics: Allows a deeper stretch at the bottom of the movement and independent arm control, correcting strength imbalances.
setup_cues: Sit on the edge of the bench with dumbbells on thighs.
Lie back, kicking dumbbells up to chest level.
Keep feet flat on the floor and shoulder blades squeezed.
Press dumbbells up, maintaining a slight inward angle.
common_mistakes: Clashing the dumbbells together at the top, losing tension.
Allowing elbows to flare excessively.
Uneven pressing speed between left and right arms.
exercises.progression: Increase dumbbell weight or perform with a brief pause at the bottom stretch.
exercises.regression: Chest press machine or light dumbbell press floor variation.

expert_rating.verdict: Allows a deeper chest stretch and free arm convergence, though setup can limit top weights.

exercises.plain_summary: Press two separate weights over your chest to build your pecs while letting your arms move in a natural path.

exercises.name: Incline Barbell Bench Press
exercises.biomechanics: Shifts the emphasis toward the upper clavicular fibers of the chest and increases anterior shoulder contribution.
setup_cues: Set the bench angle to 30-45 degrees.
Position yourself with eyes directly under the bar.
Unrack the bar and lower it controlled to the upper chest.
Press up and slightly back toward the face.
common_mistakes: Setting the incline too high (over 45 degrees), turning it into a shoulder press.
Letting the bar drift too far forward during the descent.
Arching the lower back excessively to make it a flat press.
exercises.progression: Add weight slowly while maintaining stable shoulder positioning and controlled tempos.
exercises.regression: Chest press machine or incline dumbbell press.

media.matched_name: Barbell Incline Bench Press - Medium Grip

expert_rating.verdict: Solid upper chest builder; similarly restricted by the bar path.

exercises.plain_summary: Press a barbell on an upward slope to target your upper chest, filling out the area right below your collarbone.

exercises.name: Incline Dumbbell Press
exercises.biomechanics: Provides a joint-friendly path for upper chest training, allowing natural rotation of the wrists.
setup_cues: Set incline bench to 30 degrees.
Kick dumbbells up to shoulder height while lying back.
Depress shoulders and pull them back into the bench.
Press dumbbells up in a slight arc without touching them at the top.
common_mistakes: Allowing the weights to drift outward, straining shoulders.
Bouncing the weights at the bottom stretch.
Elbows flaring out rather than tucked at a 45-degree angle.
exercises.progression: Increase weight or add a 2-second pause at the bottom of each rep.
exercises.regression: Chest press machine or decrease dumbbell weight.

expert_rating.verdict: Top-tier upper-chest developer. Joint-friendly angle allows optimal alignment with upper chest fibers.

exercises.plain_summary: Press dumbbells on a slanted bench to build your upper chest while allowing your hands to rotate naturally to protect your shoulders.

exercises.name: Incline Dumbbell Flyes
exercises.biomechanics: Isolates the chest by removing triceps involvement, focusing on horizontal adduction under stretch.
setup_cues: Lie on a 30-degree incline bench with dumbbells held overhead.
Maintain a slight bend in the elbows throughout the set.
Lower dumbbells out in a wide arc until chest feels stretched.
Squeeze chest to return dumbbells to starting position.
common_mistakes: Turning the fly into a press by bending the elbows too much at the bottom.
Lowering the weights too deep, risking shoulder injury.
Colliding the dumbbells together at the top, removing tension.
exercises.progression: Increase dumbbell weight slightly or focus on slow eccentric phases.
exercises.regression: Cable crossover or machine flyes.

expert_rating.verdict: Excellent stretch, but tension drops off to zero at the top. Cable variations are vastly superior.

exercises.plain_summary: Sweep two dumbbells out in a wide arc on a slanted bench to stretch and isolate your upper chest muscles.

exercises.name: Push-Up
exercises.biomechanics: A versatile bodyweight movement that builds horizontal press strength while requiring active core stabilization.
setup_cues: Place hands slightly wider than shoulder width on the floor.
Establish a straight line from head to heels, squeezing glutes.
Lower chest to the floor by bending elbows back at a 45-degree angle.
Push away from the floor back to the starting plank.
common_mistakes: Allowing the hips to sag, putting pressure on the lower back.
Flaring elbows to 90 degrees.
Doing half reps by not lowering chest all the way.
exercises.progression: Perform decline push-ups (feet elevated) or add weighted vest.
exercises.regression: Incline push-ups (hands on a bench or wall) or knee push-ups.

expert_rating.verdict: Excellent shoulder blade movement (scapular freedom), but difficult to overload progressively.

exercises.plain_summary: Push your body weight off the floor to build your chest, shoulders, and arms while teaching your core to stay tight.

exercises.name: Seated Chest Press Machine
exercises.biomechanics: Targets the mid-chest with a stabilized movement pattern, excellent for training close to failure safely.
setup_cues: Adjust seat so handles are at mid-chest level.
Keep shoulder blades retracted and chest up.
Push handles forward while keeping elbows tucked slightly below shoulders.
Control the weight back to the starting point without resting.
common_mistakes: Not using a full range of motion.
Letting the lower back arch away from the pad.
Flaring elbows upwards during the push.
exercises.progression: Increase weight or add a pause at the peak contraction.
exercises.regression: Decrease weight or perform standard bodyweight push-ups.

expert_rating.verdict: Highly stable, allowing safe training close to absolute muscular failure without balance constraints.

exercises.plain_summary: Push the handles of a guided machine forward to train your chest safely without needing to balance a heavy free weight.

exercises.name: Cable Crossover
exercises.biomechanics: Maintains constant tension on the chest throughout the entire range of motion, especially at peak contraction.
setup_cues: Set pulleys to shoulder height or higher.
Grab handles, step forward to create tension, and stand split-stance.
Maintain a slight elbow bend and lean forward slightly.
Bring hands together in front of the waist in a sweeping arc.
common_mistakes: Pressing the weight instead of flying.
Letting the hands go too far back and overstretching the shoulders.
Using momentum or leaning too far forward.
exercises.progression: Increase cable stack weight or add a squeeze at contraction.
exercises.regression: Reduce weight or use incline dumbbell flyes with light weights.

expert_rating.verdict: Maintains constant tension across the entire range of motion, providing a great squeeze at the top.

exercises.plain_summary: Pull cables together in front of you to keep constant tension on your chest muscles, especially when your hands meet.

exercises.name: Overhead Barbell Press
exercises.biomechanics: A fundamental vertical press that challenges shoulder strength, core stability, and overhead mobility.
setup_cues: Set bar at chest height and grip slightly wider than shoulders.
Keep forearms vertical under the bar, elbows tucked slightly.
Brace core, squeeze glutes, and press bar straight up.
Pull head back slightly as the bar passes the face, then push head forward at lock.
common_mistakes: Leaning back excessively, converting it to an incline press.
Failing to brace the core, causing lower back strain.
Not locking out at the top or skipping the bottom range.
exercises.progression: Add weight slowly or perform seated to isolate the shoulders.
exercises.regression: Seated dumbbell shoulder press or dumbbell shoulder press.

expert_rating.verdict: Excellent strength/overhead test, but high fatigue and lower back limits make it sub-optimal for shoulder growth.

exercises.plain_summary: Press a barbell straight up to build the front of your shoulders and strengthen your core as you stand tall.

exercises.name: Seated Dumbbell Shoulder Press
exercises.biomechanics: Provides independent shoulder loading, reducing core stability demands compared to standing press.
setup_cues: Sit on a bench with back support at a high angle.
Kick dumbbells up to shoulder height.
Keep elbows tucked at a 30-degree angle forward (scapular plane).
Press weights overhead in a controlled arc without touching them.
common_mistakes: Flaring elbows completely to the sides (90 degrees).
Arching lower back off the pad.
Dropping weights too fast and losing tension at the bottom.
exercises.progression: Increase dumbbell weight or pause at the bottom of the movement.
exercises.regression: Seated machine shoulder press or lighter dumbbells.

expert_rating.verdict: Far superior shoulder hypertrophy stimulus than standing barbell press due to back support and stability.

exercises.plain_summary: Press dumbbells overhead while sitting to build the front of your shoulders without putting extra strain on your lower back.

exercises.name: Dumbbell Lateral Raise
exercises.biomechanics: Isolates the side shoulders through shoulder abduction, creating upper body width.
setup_cues: Stand tall with dumbbells at your sides.
Lean forward very slightly, keeping chest proud.
Raise weights out to the sides, leading with the elbows.
Stop when hands reach shoulder height, then lower under control.
common_mistakes: Shrugging the shoulders up, transferring the load to the traps.
Using body momentum to swing the weights up.
Keeping arms completely straight, placing stress on the elbows.
exercises.progression: Increase weight slightly or use a 3-second negative tempo.
exercises.regression: Cable lateral raise or lighter dumbbells.

expert_rating.verdict: Classic lateral head isolation, but suffers from zero tension at the bottom and max tension at the top.

exercises.plain_summary: Raise dumbbells out to your sides to build your side shoulders, creating the cap that makes your upper body look wider.

exercises.name: Cable Lateral Raise
exercises.biomechanics: Maintains constant tension on the side deltoids, especially in the stretched position at the bottom of the rep.
setup_cues: Set pulley to the lowest setting.
Stand sideways to the machine, holding the handle with the far hand.
Keep a slight bend in the elbow and chest up.
Raise hand out to the side until it reaches shoulder height.
common_mistakes: Allowing the body to lean too far away from the machine.
Slamming the weights at the bottom.
Using momentum instead of controlled muscle contraction.
exercises.progression: Increase the cable stack weight or add a pause at the top.
exercises.regression: Dumbbell lateral raise with light weights.

expert_rating.verdict: Superior to dumbbells due to constant cable tension, especially overloading the lateral delts in their stretched position.

exercises.plain_summary: Pull a cable across your body to keep constant tension on your side shoulders, building width even at the very bottom.

exercises.name: Cable Tricep Pushdown
exercises.biomechanics: Isolates the triceps, particularly the lateral and medial heads, by restricting movement to elbow extension.
setup_cues: Attach a rope or straight bar to a high pulley.
Step back slightly, tucking elbows close to your ribs.
Keep chest up and knees slightly bent.
Push the weight down, fully extending the elbows and spreading the rope at the bottom.
common_mistakes: Allowing the elbows to drift forward and backward, using the chest or shoulders.
Leaning too far over the bar to use bodyweight.
Letting the wrists collapse.
exercises.progression: Increase the cable stack weight or add a hold at full extension.
exercises.regression: Reduce stack weight or use lighter resistance band pushdowns.

expert_rating.verdict: Superb lateral/medial tricep head builder. Extremely stable and easily customized.

exercises.plain_summary: Push a cable attachment down to isolate and build the triceps, which make up the back of your upper arm.

exercises.name: Overhead Dumbbell Tricep Extension
exercises.biomechanics: Overloads the long head of the triceps by placing the shoulder in a flexed, overhead position under stretch.
setup_cues: Sit on a short-backed bench and hold a dumbbell overhead with both hands.
Keep elbows tucked close to your head, pointing forward.
Lower the weight slowly behind your head.
Press the dumbbell back up to the starting position by extending the elbows.
common_mistakes: Flaring elbows wide, placing stress on the shoulder joint.
Not lowering the weight far enough to get a stretch.
Arching the lower back excessively.
exercises.progression: Increase dumbbell weight or use a single-arm variation.
exercises.regression: Cable tricep pushdown to avoid overhead shoulder mobility demands.

expert_rating.verdict: Puts the long head of the triceps in a deep stretch, capitalizing on stretch-mediated hypertrophy.

exercises.plain_summary: Stretches the long head of your triceps overhead — the position that builds the thick back of your arm.

exercises.name: Lying EZ-Bar Tricep Extension
exercises.biomechanics: Allows intense triceps loading with the shoulders fixed at 90 degrees, offering high stretch at the bottom of the movement.
setup_cues: Lie on a flat bench holding an EZ-bar or barbell above chest with arms straight.
Incline your arms back slightly (about 10 degrees) to keep constant tension.
Bend at the elbows to lower the bar toward your forehead or behind your head.
Extend the elbows to return to the starting position, keeping the upper arms locked.
common_mistakes: Allowing elbows to flare outward to the sides.
Moving the shoulders back and forth, turning it into a pull-over.
Slamming the bar toward the forehead.
exercises.progression: Increase the bar load or perform with dumbbells.
exercises.regression: Cable tricep pushdown for safer elbow loading.

expert_rating.verdict: Hits the long head under excellent load, but can cause elbow joint stress over time.

exercises.plain_summary: Lower a weight toward your forehead while lying down to stretch and load the triceps on the back of your arms.

exercises.name: Lat Pulldown
exercises.biomechanics: Trains vertical shoulder adduction and elbow flexion, overloading the lats in the mid-to-stretched range.
setup_cues: Adjust thigh pad so legs are locked in.
Grip the bar slightly wider than shoulders.
Lean back slightly (10-15 degrees) and pull shoulder blades down.
Pull the bar to your upper chest, leading with the elbows.
common_mistakes: Pulling the bar behind the neck, risking shoulder impingement.
Using body momentum to swing and pull the weight.
Letsing the shoulders shrug up at the top.
exercises.progression: Increase cable weight while keeping chest up and movement controlled.
exercises.regression: Assisted pull-ups or lighter lat pulldowns.

expert_rating.verdict: Highly stable, easily progressive vertical pull that loads the lats optimally in the stretch.

exercises.plain_summary: Pulls a bar down to train your lats, building the back width that creates a V-taper.

exercises.name: Pull-Up
exercises.biomechanics: A fundamental vertical pull that requires significant relative bodyweight strength and core stabilization.
setup_cues: Grip the bar with palms facing away, slightly wider than shoulder width.
Hang at full extension, then depress shoulder blades.
Pull chest toward the bar, driving elbows down.
Lower yourself slowly back to a dead hang.
common_mistakes: Kicking legs or using momentum (kipping).
Not completing the full range of motion (chin not clearing bar).
Allowing shoulders to roll forward at the top.
exercises.progression: Add weight via a dip belt or slow down the eccentric phase.
exercises.regression: Assisted pull-up or lat pulldowns.

expert_rating.verdict: Classic vertical pull, but bodyweight limitation makes incremental loading less smooth.

exercises.plain_summary: Pull your own body weight up to a bar to build your lats, the big wing-shaped muscles on your back.

exercises.name: Assisted Pull-Up
exercises.biomechanics: Allows building vertical pulling strength with reduced load, ensuring proper form and lat activation.
setup_cues: Set the counterweight pad and stand/kneel on it.
Grip the handles slightly wider than shoulders.
Depress shoulder blades and pull chest up toward the handles.
Control the descent back to the starting point.
common_mistakes: Bouncing at the bottom of the movement.
Using too much assistance and not challenging the muscles.
Allowing the chest to cave at the top.
exercises.progression: Gradually decrease the assistance weight on the machine.
exercises.regression: Increase the assistance weight or perform lat pulldowns.

expert_rating.verdict: More scalable and controllable version of the pull-up, allowing strict lat isolation.

exercises.plain_summary: Use a counterweight platform to help pull yourself up, building back width through your lats with a manageable load.

exercises.name: Seated Cable Row
exercises.biomechanics: A versatile horizontal pull that targets upper back thickness and shoulder blade retraction.
setup_cues: Sit on the bench, knees slightly bent, and grip the attachment.
Sit upright, shoulders back and down, core braced.
Pull the handle toward the lower sternum, squeezing shoulder blades.
Extend arms forward under control, keeping the torso stable.
common_mistakes: Leaning excessively backward and forward, using lower back momentum.
Shrugging shoulders up toward ears.
Failing to squeeze shoulder blades at the end of the pull.
exercises.progression: Increase cable stack weight or add a 1-second pause at peak contraction.
exercises.regression: Chest-supported row machine or lighter cable weight.

expert_rating.verdict: Stable horizontal pull allowing great shoulder blade retraction and middle-back loading.

exercises.plain_summary: Rows a handle to your waist to thicken your mid-back — the muscles that fill out the V from behind.

exercises.name: Chest-Supported Row Machine
exercises.biomechanics: Removes lower back stabilization requirements, allowing complete focus on isolating the upper back and lats.
setup_cues: Adjust seat so the chest pad is resting against the middle of your sternum.
Keep chest flat on the pad, feet firmly planted.
Grip the handles and pull them toward you, driving elbows back.
Control the weight back to the start, feeling the stretch in your lats.
common_mistakes: Lifting the chest off the pad during the pull.
Letting shoulders roll forward at the end of the movement.
Slamming the weights.
exercises.progression: Increase machine load or perform with single-arm focus.
exercises.regression: Decrease weight or perform seated cable rows.

expert_rating.verdict: Top-tier back builder. Chest support completely removes lower back limits, letting you isolate the upper back or lats.

exercises.plain_summary: Pull machine handles with your chest resting on a pad to isolate your upper back muscles without straining your spine.

exercises.name: Single-Arm Dumbbell Row
exercises.biomechanics: Allows unilateral back training to address strength discrepancies, with high lat engagement through a long range of motion.
setup_cues: Place one knee and hand on the bench, keeping the back flat and parallel to floor.
Hold the dumbbell in the opposite hand, arm hanging straight down.
Pull the dumbbell up to your hip, keeping the elbow tucked.
Lower the weight slowly to the start position, feeling a lat stretch.
common_mistakes: Twisting the torso to help pull the dumbbell.
Pulling the dumbbell to the chest instead of the hip.
Rounding the lower back.
exercises.progression: Increase dumbbell weight or focus on a slow, 3-second eccentric phase.
exercises.regression: Chest-supported row machine or lighter dumbbells.

expert_rating.verdict: Excellent single-arm row that provides a deep lat stretch, though core rotation can creep in.

exercises.plain_summary: Pull a dumbbell to your hip one side at a time to build your back width and balance strength between arms.

exercises.name: Bent-Over Barbell Row
exercises.biomechanics: A compound back builder that requires significant isometric lower-back and hamstring engagement.
setup_cues: Stand with feet hip-width apart and hinge forward at the hips to about 45 degrees.
Grip the barbell slightly wider than shoulders.
Keep the spine neutral and pull the bar to your belly button.
Lower the bar under control back to arm's length.
common_mistakes: Rounding the back, risking lower back injury.
Standing too upright, turning it into a shoulder press.
Using leg momentum to lift the bar.
exercises.progression: Increase bar weight or incorporate pauses at the top.
exercises.regression: Chest-supported row machine or single-arm dumbbell row.

expert_rating.verdict: Great for overall strength, but highly limited by spinal erector fatigue rather than upper back fatigue.

exercises.plain_summary: Bend forward and pull a barbell to your stomach to build thickness in your upper back and strengthen your posture.

exercises.name: Cable Face Pull
exercises.biomechanics: Combines horizontal pulling with shoulder external rotation, critical for posture and shoulder health.
setup_cues: Set pulley at upper chest/face height with a rope attachment.
Hold the rope with thumbs pointing back.
Step back to tension cable, standing split-stance.
Pull the rope toward your nose, flaring elbows out and pulling hands apart at the end.
common_mistakes: Pulling too low toward the chest, missing the rear delts.
Using too much weight, causing shrugging or leaning back.
Slamming the stack.
exercises.progression: Increase cable stack weight slowly while keeping strict form.
exercises.regression: Decrease weight or perform band pull-aparts.

expert_rating.verdict: Outstanding for rear delts, lower traps, and general rotator cuff/shoulder health.

exercises.plain_summary: Pull a cable rope toward your face to strengthen your rear shoulders and upper back, helping pull your shoulders back.

exercises.name: Reverse Dumbbell Fly
exercises.biomechanics: Isolates the rear shoulder by performing horizontal abduction, preventing shoulder imbalance.
setup_cues: Hinge forward at the hips with flat back, or lie chest-down on a low incline bench.
Hold dumbbells beneath you with arms slightly bent.
Raise weights out to the sides in a wide arc, leading with knuckles.
Lower under control back to the starting point.
common_mistakes: Squeezing the shoulder blades too early, letting traps dominate rear delts.
Swinging the dumbbells using hip momentum.
Bending the elbows too much, making it a row.
exercises.progression: Increase dumbbell weight slightly or add a pause at the peak.
exercises.regression: Cable face pulls or lighter dumbbells.

expert_rating.verdict: Good rear-delt builder, though tension is unevenly distributed through the arc.

exercises.plain_summary: Raise dumbbells out to the sides while bent forward to isolate the rear shoulders, which helps balance your posture.

exercises.name: Close-Grip Lat Pulldown
exercises.biomechanics: Using a neutral, close-grip attachment places the arms in shoulder extension, increasing pull through the lower lats.
setup_cues: Attach a close-grip V-bar to the lat pulldown station.
Slide knees under pad and grip the handle.
Lean back slightly and pull the handle to your chest, driving elbows down.
Extend arms fully, letting lats stretch at the top.
common_mistakes: Pulling with the arms rather than driving with the elbows.
Rounding the chest and shoulders forward at the bottom.
Leaning too far back to pull the weight.
exercises.progression: Increase cable weight while keeping lats engaged and torso stable.
exercises.regression: Perform standard lat pulldown with lighter load.

expert_rating.verdict: Close grip puts the lats in an excellent line of pull, leading to deep stretch and high activation.

exercises.plain_summary: Pull a narrow handle down to your chest to focus on the lower section of your lats near the waist.

exercises.name: Standing Dumbbell Curl
exercises.biomechanics: Isolates elbow flexion and forearm supination, targeting the biceps.
setup_cues: Stand tall with dumbbells at your sides, palms facing each other.
Squeeze elbows close to your torso.
Curl weights up, rotating wrists so palms face up at the top.
Lower dumbbells slowly to the starting position.
common_mistakes: Swinging the body to lift the weights.
Letting elbows drift forward, engaging the anterior shoulder.
Not extending arms fully at the bottom.
exercises.progression: Increase dumbbell weight or perform seated to prevent swinging.
exercises.regression: Cable bicep curl or lighter dumbbells.

expert_rating.verdict: A baseline staple. Supinating the wrist at the top aligns with the biceps' main functions.

exercises.plain_summary: Curl weights up to your shoulders to squeeze and build your biceps, the muscles on the front of your arms.

exercises.name: Hammer Curl
exercises.biomechanics: Using a neutral grip shifts the load to the brachialis and brachioradialis, building forearm and upper-arm thickness.
setup_cues: Stand tall with dumbbells in hands, palms facing inward.
Keep elbows pinned to your sides.
Curl the dumbbells up while maintaining the neutral (hammer) grip.
Lower slowly back to full extension.
common_mistakes: Using hip momentum to get the dumbbells moving.
Elbows drifting forward during the curl.
Half-repping by stopping short of full extension.
exercises.progression: Increase dumbbell weight or use slow eccentric tempo.
exercises.regression: Cable hammer curls with rope attachment or lighter dumbbells.

expert_rating.verdict: Essential for building forearm thickness and upper-arm width by targeting brachialis and brachioradialis.

exercises.plain_summary: Curl dumbbells with your palms facing each other to target your forearms and the muscle that sits under your biceps.

exercises.name: Incline Dumbbell Curl
exercises.biomechanics: Placing the shoulders in hyperextension puts the bicep long head under a high passive stretch, increasing recruitment.
setup_cues: Set incline bench to 45 degrees.
Sit back, letting dumbbells hang straight down behind the torso.
Keep elbows fixed in place and curl the weights up.
Lower dumbbells slowly to feel the deep stretch at the bottom.
common_mistakes: Allowing the elbows to swing forward to make the curl easier.
Using a bench incline that is too steep or too low.
Not completing the full stretch at the bottom.
exercises.progression: Increase dumbbell weight slightly or hold the stretch at the bottom.
exercises.regression: Standing dumbbell curl to remove the intense stretch position.

expert_rating.verdict: Unrivaled stretch-mediated bicep builder. Keeps constant tension on the long head in its most lengthened position.

exercises.plain_summary: Curl weights while sitting back on a slanted bench to stretch and build the outer peak of your biceps.

exercises.name: Preacher EZ-Bar Curl
exercises.biomechanics: The arm pad prevents shoulder movement, isolating the biceps and highlighting peak contraction in the shortened range.
setup_cues: Sit at the bench, placing your armpits flat against the top of the pad.
Grip the bar with palms facing up.
Lower the bar slowly until arms are almost fully straight.
Curl the bar up toward your face, keeping elbows firmly on the pad.
common_mistakes: Hyperextending the elbows at the bottom, risking tendon injury.
Lifting the armpits or chest off the pad.
Not going through the full range of motion.
exercises.progression: Increase EZ bar load slowly while keeping 1-3 reps in reserve.
exercises.regression: Standing dumbbell curls or machine preacher curls with light weights.

expert_rating.verdict: Arm support removes momentum, creating strict tension, but overloading is heaviest at the bottom extension.

exercises.plain_summary: Rest your arms on a slanted pad while curling to prevent cheating and target the inner part of your biceps.

exercises.name: Cable Bicep Curl
exercises.biomechanics: Provides constant tension on the biceps throughout the movement, avoiding the drop-offs in tension typical of free weights.
setup_cues: Set pulley to the bottom setting with a bar or rope attachment.
Stand facing the machine, elbows tucked at sides.
Curl the handle up to shoulder level.
Lower under control, fully extending arms.
common_mistakes: Standing too far back, changing the angle of pull.
Letting elbows flare or move forward.
Slamming the weight stack.
exercises.progression: Increase stack weight or add a 1-second pause at contraction.
exercises.regression: Decrease stack weight or use dumbbell curls.

expert_rating.verdict: Constant tension throughout the entire movement arc, preventing rest at the bottom or top.

exercises.plain_summary: Curl a cable bar up to keep smooth, constant tension on your biceps all the way through the movement.

exercises.name: Barbell Back Squat
exercises.biomechanics: A primary compound lower-body movement that loads quads, glutes, and core under high mechanical tension.
setup_cues: Set bar at chest height and step under, resting it across upper back/traps.
Step back, setting feet slightly wider than hips, toes out 15-30 degrees.
Brace core and sit down between knees, keeping chest proud.
Drive through the mid-foot to stand up, keeping knees aligned with toes.
common_mistakes: Allowing knees to cave inward (valgus collapse).
Rounding the spine or chest collapsing forward.
Squatting too shallow (not reaching parallel).
exercises.progression: Increase bar weight slowly while maintaining deep depth and clean form.
exercises.regression: Goblet squats or leg press to build lower-body capacity with less spine loading.

expert_rating.verdict: Amazing strength movement, but systemic/lower-back fatigue limits direct quad growth compared to hack squats.

exercises.plain_summary: Bend your knees with a barbell on your back to build your quads, glutes, and overall lower body power.

exercises.name: Goblet Squat
exercises.biomechanics: An excellent squat pattern that uses front-loading to encourage a vertical torso, reducing back shear.
setup_cues: Hold a dumbbell vertically by the upper bell, close to chest.
Stand with feet shoulder-width apart.
Squat down by pushing hips back and knees out, keeping elbows inside knees.
Drive back to the top, keeping core braced.
common_mistakes: Holding the dumbbell away from the chest, straining arms.
Letting knees collapse inward.
Rounding the upper back at the bottom.
exercises.progression: Increase dumbbell weight or add a pause at the bottom.
exercises.regression: Bodyweight squat or goblet box squat.

expert_rating.verdict: Great for learning squat mechanics, but loading is limited by how much weight your arms can support.

exercises.plain_summary: Hold a weight against your chest while squatting to keep your torso upright and target the front of your thighs.

exercises.name: Leg Press
exercises.biomechanics: Removes balance and spinal loading constraints, allowing safe, high-load hypertrophy training for quads and glutes.
setup_cues: Sit in machine, lower back flat against backrest.
Place feet shoulder-width apart on the sled.
Release safety locks and lower sled slowly toward chest until knees are at 90 degrees.
Press the sled away, stopping just short of locking knees.
common_mistakes: Lowering the sled too deep, causing the tailbone to lift off the pad (butt wink).
Locking knees aggressively at the top.
Placing feet too low or high without proper alignment.
exercises.progression: Increase machine load while maintaining a controlled tempo.
exercises.regression: Reduce machine weight or perform goblet squats.

expert_rating.verdict: Superb quad hypertrophy tool. High stability removes back limitation, letting you load the quads deep in the stretch.

exercises.plain_summary: Push a heavy sled away with your feet to build your thighs and glutes without loading weight onto your spine.

exercises.name: Romanian Deadlift
exercises.biomechanics: An essential hip hinge movement that overloads the posterior chain in the stretched position.
setup_cues: Stand holding barbell/dumbbells at thighs, feet hip-width apart.
Brace core, soften knees, and push hips straight back.
Keep the weight close to your legs as you lower it toward mid-shin.
Squeeze glutes and drive hips forward to stand, keeping spine straight.
common_mistakes: Allowing the bar to drift away from the legs, stressing the lower back.
Rounding the lower or upper back.
Bending knees too much, turning the hinge into a squat.
exercises.progression: Increase bar weight or perform with a slow eccentric phase.
exercises.regression: Seated leg curl to train hamstrings without lower-back loading.

expert_rating.verdict: The gold standard for posterior chain hypertrophy. Overloads the hamstrings and glutes under deep eccentric stretch.

exercises.plain_summary: Hinge at your hips to lower a barbell, stretching and strengthening the back of your thighs and your glutes.

exercises.name: Barbell Conventional Deadlift
exercises.biomechanics: A primary compound movement pulling from the floor, building overall body strength and posterior chain power.
setup_cues: Stand with mid-foot under the bar, feet hip-width.
Hinge down, gripping the bar outside shins.
Pull shins forward to touch the bar, flatten back, and pull shoulder blades back.
Drive legs into floor to stand up, keeping bar close to shins.
common_mistakes: Rounding the back during the lift, risking disc injury.
Jerk-starting the lift instead of pulling tension out of the bar first.
Hyperextending the lower back at the top.
exercises.progression: Increase bar weight slowly or transition to trap bar deadlifts.
exercises.regression: Romanian deadlift or rack pulls.

expert_rating.verdict: Excellent whole-body power builder, but poor stimulus-to-fatigue ratio due to lack of eccentric control and high fatigue.

exercises.plain_summary: Lift a heavy barbell off the floor to build total body strength, focusing on your glutes, hamstrings, and back.

exercises.name: Seated Leg Curl
exercises.biomechanics: Isolates the hamstrings in a seated position where the hip is flexed, putting hamstrings in a greater stretched state.
setup_cues: Sit in machine, aligning knee joint with the machine pivot point.
Secure thigh pad firmly against thighs.
Place feet on top of roller, pull toes up.
Curl legs down and back, squeezing hamstrings at the bottom.
Return under control, feeling a stretch.
common_mistakes: Letting the butt lift off the seat during the curl.
Allowing the weight stack to slam at the top.
Using a fast, uncontrolled tempo.
exercises.progression: Increase stack weight or add a 1-second pause at full contraction.
exercises.regression: Lighter stack weight or lying leg curl.

expert_rating.verdict: Top-tier hamstring builder. Seated posture flexes the hips, placing hamstrings in a maximally stretched state.

exercises.plain_summary: Bend your knees against machine resistance while sitting to isolate and build the back of your thighs under a deep stretch.

exercises.name: Lying Leg Curl
exercises.biomechanics: Isolates the hamstrings with the hips extended, focusing on the knee flexion function.
setup_cues: Lie face down on the machine, placing roller pad just below calf muscles.
Hold handles and press hips down into the pad.
Curl heels toward glutes in a smooth arc.
Slowly extend legs back to the starting position.
common_mistakes: Arching the lower back or lifting hips off the pad to assist the curl.
Swinging the weight up.
Not going through a full range of motion.
exercises.progression: Increase machine load or perform unilaterally.
exercises.regression: Seated leg curl or reduce weight.

expert_rating.verdict: Isolates hamstrings, but offers slightly less growth stimulus than seated curls due to neutral hips.

exercises.plain_summary: Bend your legs while lying flat to isolate and strengthen your hamstrings, the muscles along the back of your thighs.

exercises.name: Leg Extension
exercises.biomechanics: Isolates the quadriceps, specifically overloading them in the shortened, fully contracted range.
setup_cues: Sit in machine, back supported, placing roller pad at top of shins.
Align knee joint with machine pivot point.
Hold handles to stabilize torso.
Extend legs fully, flexing quads at the top, then lower under control.
common_mistakes: Slamming the weights or rushing the eccentric phase.
Allowing hips to rise off the seat.
Pointing or flexing toes excessively in a way that shifts knee tension awkwardly.
exercises.progression: Increase machine weight or pause for 2 seconds at full extension.
exercises.regression: Decrease machine weight or perform goblet squats.

expert_rating.verdict: The only exercise that isolates the rectus femoris (quad) under peak contraction. Excellent stability.

exercises.plain_summary: Straighten your legs against a padded roller while seated to isolate and burn the muscles on the front of your thighs.

exercises.name: Barbell Hip Thrust
exercises.biomechanics: Overloads the glutes in their fully shortened position under high horizontal mechanical tension.
setup_cues: Sit on floor, upper back against a secured bench.
Roll a padded barbell over hips and plant feet flat.
Drive heels into floor and lift hips, keeping chin tucked and ribs down.
Squeeze glutes at the top (hips aligned with knees), then lower slowly.
common_mistakes: Arching the lower back at the top instead of tilting the pelvis.
Placing feet too far forward (hamstring dominant) or too close (quad dominant).
Letting the neck fly back instead of keeping chin tucked.
exercises.progression: Add weight to the barbell or add a pause at the top.
exercises.regression: Glute bridge (bodyweight on floor) or single-leg glute bridge.

expert_rating.verdict: Excellent peak contraction glute overload, but setup can be tedious and fatigue-inducing.

exercises.plain_summary: Drive your hips upward with a loaded barbell across your lap to isolate and strengthen your glutes, your rear muscles.

exercises.name: Bulgarian Split Squat
exercises.biomechanics: A highly effective unilateral lower-body exercise that develops single-leg strength and stability while deep-stretching the hip flexor.
setup_cues: Stand in front of a bench, placing the top of one foot flat on the bench behind you.
Hold dumbbells at your sides.
Lower rear knee toward the floor, keeping front knee tracking in line with front foot.
Drive back up through the front heel.
common_mistakes: Placing the front foot too close to the bench, compressing the knee.
Allowing the front knee to cave inward.
Torso collapsing excessively forward.
exercises.progression: Increase dumbbell weight or perform with a deficit (front foot elevated).
exercises.regression: Dumbbell lunges or bodyweight split squats.

expert_rating.verdict: Incredible quad and glute builder under stretch. Unilateral isolation is fantastic, though balance can be tricky.

exercises.plain_summary: Elevate one foot behind you and squat to target your front leg, building single-leg balance, quads, and glutes.

exercises.name: Dumbbell Lunges
exercises.biomechanics: A dynamic unilateral movement that trains deceleration, hip stability, and knee control.
setup_cues: Stand tall holding dumbbells at your sides.
Take a controlled step forward, lowering hips until back knee is near the floor.
Keep front knee tracking over front toes.
Push off the front foot to return to the starting position.
common_mistakes: Walking a tightrope (stepping inline), losing balance.
Slamming the rear knee into the floor.
Allowing front knee to drift far past toes without heel support.
exercises.progression: Increase dumbbell weight or switch to reverse lunges (safer for knees).
exercises.regression: Bodyweight lunges or static split squats.

expert_rating.verdict: Dynamic athletic movement, but balance requirements reduce absolute target muscle loading.

exercises.plain_summary: Step forward and lower your hips to train your thighs and glutes one leg at a time, improving stability.

exercises.name: Standing Calf Raise
exercises.biomechanics: Overloads the gastrocnemius calf muscle by performing ankle plantarflexion with a straight knee.
setup_cues: Place balls of feet on step, heels hanging off, knees locked straight.
Lower heels down slowly to feel a deep stretch in the calves.
Push up through the big toe to raise heels as high as possible.
Hold for 1 second at the top, then lower controlled.
common_mistakes: Bouncing at the bottom, using Achilles tendon elasticity instead of muscle.
Bending the knees to push the weight.
Not using a full range of motion.
exercises.progression: Increase weight or add a 2-second pause at the bottom stretch.
exercises.regression: Bodyweight standing calf raises on a flat floor.
exercises.planning_note: Pick standing or seated calf raises based on the athlete's gym equipment.

expert_rating.verdict: Essential for calf gastrocnemius growth; requires a deep stretch hold at the bottom.

exercises.plain_summary: Raise up onto your toes while standing to build the outer calf muscle, giving your lower legs shape.

exercises.name: Seated Calf Raise
exercises.biomechanics: Since the knee is bent, the gastrocnemius is active-insufficient, isolating the deeper soleus calf muscle.
setup_cues: Sit in machine and adjust thigh pad over knees.
Place balls of feet on the platform.
Release safety bar and lower heels down slowly for a stretch.
Press up through toes to elevate knees, contracting calves.
common_mistakes: Bouncing the weight stack.
Using hands to pull thighs up.
Failing to stretch fully at the bottom.
exercises.progression: Increase machine weight slowly while maintaining controlled pauses.
exercises.regression: Standing calf raises with bodyweight.

expert_rating.verdict: Isolates the soleus (lower calf) because the bent knee deactivates the larger gastrocnemius muscle.

exercises.plain_summary: Push up on your toes while sitting to isolate the deep calf muscle that sits underneath the outer cap.

exercises.name: Back Extension
exercises.biomechanics: Strengthens the posterior chain, specifically targeting the erector spinae, glutes, and hamstrings through hip extension.
setup_cues: Position yourself in the back extension bench, placing hips just above the pad.
Hinge forward at the hips, keeping the spine neutral.
Squeeze the glutes and hamstrings to raise your torso back to alignment.
Avoid hyperextending the lower back at the top.
common_mistakes: Hyperextending the lumbar spine at the top of the movement.
Using momentum or swinging the torso.
Bending at the waist instead of the hips.
exercises.progression: Hold a weight plate or dumbbell at the chest.
exercises.regression: Bodyweight back extensions or decrease range of motion.

expert_rating.verdict: Great for isolating hip extension and lumbar erectors with minimal fatigue compared to deadlifts.

exercises.plain_summary: Raise your torso from a bent position on a bench to strengthen your lower back, glutes, and back of thighs.

exercises.name: Trap Bar Deadlift
exercises.biomechanics: Allows a more vertical torso and higher quad involvement than a straight barbell, reducing lower-back shearing force.
setup_cues: Step inside the trap bar, aligning feet with the handles.
Squat/hinge down and grip handles firmly.
Flatten back and keep chest proud, bracing core.
Drive through feet to stand up, locking out hips at the top.
common_mistakes: Letting the knees cave inward.
Rounding the spine.
Hyperextending the lower back at the lockout.
exercises.progression: Add weight to the bar slowly while keeping form clean.
exercises.regression: Romanian deadlift or high-handle setup.

expert_rating.verdict: A hybrid hinge/squat that is easier on the back than conventional pulls and hits quads harder.

exercises.plain_summary: Lift a hexagonal bar while standing inside it to build your thighs and hips with less strain on your back.

exercises.name: Goblet Box Squat
exercises.biomechanics: Provides a physical depth target and breaks the eccentric-concentric cycle, building power out of the hole and teaching proper squat mechanics.
setup_cues: Stand in front of a bench/box, holding a dumbbell at chest.
Push hips back and lower until glutes touch the box lightly.
Pause for 1 second on the box without relaxing the core.
Drive heels into floor to stand up, squeezing glutes.
common_mistakes: Rocking or leaning forward to stand up off the box.
Plop-sitting (collapsing onto the box).
Allowing knees to cave.
exercises.progression: Increase dumbbell weight or lower the box height.
exercises.regression: Bodyweight squats to a high box.

expert_rating.verdict: Good squat regression, but pausing on the box dissipates stored elastic energy and tension.

exercises.plain_summary: Squat down until you touch a box, then stand up, to learn good squat form and build your thighs.

exercises.name: Forearm Plank
exercises.biomechanics: Trains isometric anterior core stability, protecting the lumbar spine from extension.
setup_cues: Place forearms on the floor, elbows directly under shoulders.
Extend legs back and lift hips, forming a straight line.
Squeeze glutes, pull belly button to spine, and press floor away with elbows.
Hold position, breathing shallowly into the stomach.
common_mistakes: Allowing the hips to sag, putting load on the lower back.
Poking hips high in the air, removing core tension.
Looking forward instead of down, straining the neck.
exercises.progression: Increase duration or perform dynamic variations (e.g. plank jacks).
exercises.regression: Knee plank or incline plank (hands on bench).

expert_rating.verdict: Decent baseline stability builder, but static isometric hold is poor for direct abdominal hypertrophy.

exercises.plain_summary: Hold a push-up position on your forearms to build endurance in your abs and keep your spine stable.

exercises.name: Dead Bug
exercises.biomechanics: Teaches coordination and core stabilization during limb movement, critical for lumbar spine safety.
setup_cues: Lie on back, arms pointing up, knees bent at 90 degrees directly over hips.
Press lower back flat against the floor (no gap).
Slowly lower right arm back and left leg forward until they hover just above floor.
Return to start and repeat with opposite limbs, maintaining flat back.
common_mistakes: Allowing the lower back to arch off the floor.
Moving the non-working limbs at the same time.
Rushing through the movement.
exercises.progression: Add light resistance bands or dumbbells.
exercises.regression: Heel taps (keeping knees bent and only tapping one heel down at a time).

expert_rating.verdict: Incredible for deep core stability (transversus abdominis) and anti-extension lumbar control.

exercises.plain_summary: Lie on your back and move opposite limbs to train your deep core muscles, protecting your spine during daily movements.

exercises.name: Cable Pallof Press
exercises.biomechanics: An anti-rotation exercise that challenges the obliques and deep stabilizers to resist lateral trunk twisting.
setup_cues: Set pulley to chest height and hold handle with both hands.
Step away from machine sideways, standing with feet shoulder-width.
Pull handle to center of chest, bracing core and squeezing glutes.
Press the cable straight out in front of you, resist pulling toward machine, and return slowly.
common_mistakes: Letting the torso twist toward the cable machine.
Shrugging shoulders or holding breath.
Using too much weight, causing hips to shift.
exercises.progression: Increase stack weight or narrow the stance.
exercises.regression: Reduce weight or use a resistance band instead of cables.

expert_rating.verdict: Outstanding anti-rotation exercise, teaching oblique/core engagement without shearing forces.

exercises.plain_summary: Press a cable out in front of you while resisting the pull to strengthen your side abs against twisting.

exercises.name: Hanging Knee Raise
exercises.biomechanics: Trains posterior pelvic tilt and hip flexion under hanging traction, strengthening the lower abs.
setup_cues: Hang from pull-up bar (or support yourself in captain's chair).
Keep shoulder blades depressed and core tight.
Raise knees toward chest by curling the pelvis upward.
Lower knees slowly under control, preventing body swing.
common_mistakes: Swinging the legs to use momentum.
Letting the shoulders shrug up or lower back arch at the bottom.
Dropping legs too fast.
exercises.progression: Perform hanging leg raise (straight legs) or hold a light dumbbell between feet.
exercises.regression: Lying leg raises on floor or captain's chair knee raises.

expert_rating.verdict: Highly effective for lower rectus abdominis, provided you actively tilt the pelvis upward at the top.

exercises.plain_summary: Hang from a bar and raise your knees to your chest to target your lower abs under traction.

exercises.name: Russian Twist
exercises.biomechanics: Trains rotational core strength and stability, targeting the internal and external obliques.
setup_cues: Sit on floor, knees bent, leaning back at a 45-degree angle.
Clasp hands in front of chest.
Rotate torso from side to side, touching hands to the floor next to your hips.
Keep spine long and chest up.
common_mistakes: Only moving the arms rather than rotating the shoulders/torso.
Rounding the upper back significantly.
Twisting too rapidly without control.
exercises.progression: Hold a light dumbbell/plate or lift feet off the floor.
exercises.regression: Keep feet planted flat on floor or reduce torso angle.

expert_rating.verdict: Good oblique rotative idea, but frequently performed with high momentum and lower back shear.

exercises.plain_summary: Twist your torso side to side while sitting on the floor to build and strengthen your side abs.

exercises.name: Ab Wheel Rollout
exercises.biomechanics: An advanced anti-extension exercise that overloads the rectus abdominis in a long, stretched position.
setup_cues: Kneel on a pad with hands on the ab wheel handles.
Start with wheel under shoulders, round the spine slightly, brace core.
Roll wheel forward, keeping core locked, until torso is near floor.
Pull wheel back to start by contracting abs, not hips.
common_mistakes: Letting the lower back arch, causing severe lower-back stress.
Leading with the hips instead of the wheel.
Bending arms during the rollout.
exercises.progression: Increase rollout distance or perform from feet.
exercises.regression: Stability ball rollout or partial-range rollout facing a wall to block the wheel.

expert_rating.verdict: Extreme anti-extension load. Smashes the rectus abdominis under stretch, but has a high entry barrier.

exercises.plain_summary: Roll a wheel forward on your knees to stretch and load your abs in a long, fully extended position.

exercises.name: Rowing Machine Warmup
exercises.biomechanics: Engages both upper and lower body in a low-impact rhythmic pattern to raise core body temperature.
setup_cues: Set damper to a moderate level (3-5).
Secure feet in straps and grip handle with straight arms.
Push with legs first, then lean back slightly, then pull handle to upper ribs.
Extend arms, lean forward, then bend knees to slide forward.
common_mistakes: Pulling with the arms first before driving with the legs.
Rounding the back at the start of the stroke.
Setting the damper too high.
exercises.progression: Slightly increase pace or stroke rate.
exercises.regression: Perform slowly at a conversational pace.
exercises.plain_summary: Row with legs and arms together to warm up your whole body and raise your heart rate before lifting.

exercises.name: Stationary Bike Warmup
exercises.biomechanics: A low-impact cardio warmup that increases knee joint synovial fluid and elevates heart rate.
setup_cues: Adjust seat height so leg is almost fully extended at the bottom of the pedal stroke.
Keep chest up and grip handles lightly.
Pedal at a moderate, consistent cadence (70-90 RPM).
Breathe deeply through the nose.
common_mistakes: Setting seat too low, causing knee strain.
Slouching heavily over the handlebars.
Using too high resistance for a warmup.
exercises.progression: Slightly increase resistance or RPM.
exercises.regression: Reduce resistance and pedal slowly.
exercises.plain_summary: Pedal a stationary bike to warm up your knees and get blood flowing to your thigh muscles and hips.

exercises.name: Treadmill Walk Warmup
exercises.biomechanics: Increases systemic circulation and prepares the ankles, knees, and hips for weight-bearing exercises.
setup_cues: Set incline to 1.0-2.0% to mimic outdoor walking.
Walk at a brisk, comfortable pace.
Swing arms naturally at your sides.
Focus on heel-to-toe foot placement.
common_mistakes: Holding onto the handrails, reducing core activity.
Walking with a slouched posture.
Setting the speed too fast too early.
exercises.progression: Increase speed or incline slightly.
exercises.regression: Decrease speed or flat walk.
exercises.plain_summary: Walk at a brisk pace on a treadmill to warm up your joints and increase blood flow before training.

exercises.name: Dynamic Arm Swings
exercises.biomechanics: Lubricates the shoulder joint and increases blood flow to the chest, back, and shoulders.
setup_cues: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, arms extended to the sides.
Swing arms across the front of your chest, crossing them over each other.
Swing back out to a stretch, then cross again with opposite arm on top.
Perform in a slow, controlled rhythm, not forcing the range.
common_mistakes: Swinging with excessive speed or aggression.
Shrugging the shoulders up toward the ears.
Rounding the upper spine.
exercises.progression: Incorporate light resistance bands for shoulder external rotation.
exercises.regression: Perform sitting down or with smaller range of motion.
exercises.plain_summary: Swing your arms in wide circles and side to side to loosen up your chest and shoulder joints.

exercises.name: Dynamic Leg Swings
exercises.biomechanics: Improves hip mobility in sagittal and frontal planes, preparing lower limbs for squats and hinges.
setup_cues: Stand next to a rack or wall, placing one hand on it for support.
Swing the outer leg forward and backward in a smooth motion.
Maintain a tall torso, resisting excessive lower-back arching.
Repeat sideways (across the body and out to the side) to warm up hip adductors.
common_mistakes: Leaning the torso forward and backward to force leg height.
Swinging aggressively, straining the hamstring.
Letting the supporting leg collapse inward.
exercises.progression: Gradually increase the range of swing as muscles warm up.
exercises.regression: Perform slow knee circles (hip openers) instead of swings.
exercises.plain_summary: Swing your legs forward and backward to stretch and warm up your hips, thighs, and hamstrings before squatting.

exercises.name: Doorway Chest Stretch
exercises.biomechanics: Stretches the chest and front shoulders, counteracting the internally rotated posture from desk work.
setup_cues: Stand in a doorway or next to a rack post.
Place your forearm flat against the surface, elbow bent at 90 degrees at shoulder height.
Step forward with one foot until a comfortable stretch is felt in the chest.
Hold and take deep diaphragmatic breaths.
common_mistakes: Leaning forward with the head, straining the neck.
Arching the lower back excessively.
Shrugging the shoulder of the stretched side.
exercises.progression: Adjust arm height higher or lower to target different chest fibers.
exercises.regression: Perform with hands behind the head, pulling elbows back gently.
exercises.plain_summary: Lean forward through a doorway to stretch your chest and front shoulders, correcting tight posture from sitting at desks.

exercises.name: Overhead Tricep Stretch
exercises.biomechanics: Lengthens the triceps and lats in shoulder flexion, improving overhead mobility.
setup_cues: Raise one arm overhead and bend the elbow, reaching hand down your spine.
Use the opposite hand to gently pull the elbow back and down.
Keep the chest up and look forward, not down.
Breath deeply to relax the target muscles.
common_mistakes: Tucking chin to chest, putting pressure on cervical spine.
Arching the lower back to compensate for tight shoulders.
Pulling too aggressively, causing pain.
exercises.progression: Incorporate a slight side bend to increase lat stretch.
exercises.regression: Cross-body tricep/shoulder stretch.
exercises.plain_summary: Pull your elbow behind your head to stretch the back of your upper arms and your wide back muscles.

exercises.name: World's Greatest Stretch
exercises.biomechanics: A comprehensive full-body mobility flow targeting hip extension, hamstring flexibility, and thoracic rotation.
setup_cues: Step back into a deep lunge with hands flat on the floor inside front foot.
Elbow-drop the hand closest to front foot toward floor, stretching hip.
Rotate that same arm upward toward ceiling, looking at your hand to open chest.
Place hand back down, push hips back to straighten front leg, stretching hamstring.
common_mistakes: Letting the back knee sag or touch the floor during the active phase.
Rounding the upper back during thoracic rotation.
Rushing through the positions instead of pausing for breaths.
exercises.progression: Increase hold time in each phase or add dynamic lateral lunges.
exercises.regression: Perform with the back knee resting on a soft pad.
exercises.plain_summary: Perform a deep lunge and twist to stretch your hips, back of your thighs, and open your upper back.

exercises.name: Foam Rolling Quads
exercises.biomechanics: Utilizes mechanical pressure to improve blood flow, down-regulate nervous system tone, and reduce muscle soreness.
setup_cues: Lie face down with a foam roller under your thighs.
Support body weight on forearms in a plank position.
Slowly roll up and down from the hip down to just above the knee.
Pause and breathe on any particularly tender spots.
common_mistakes: Rolling directly over the knee cap.
Rolling too fast, which reduces effectiveness.
Tensing the muscles instead of relaxing them into the roller.
exercises.progression: Cross one leg over the other to increase pressure on a single side.
exercises.regression: Roll both legs together to distribute pressure, or use a slower tempo/softer roller.
exercises.plain_summary: Roll your thighs over a foam roller to massage and loosen tight quad muscles and ease muscle soreness.

exercises.name: Classic Sit-Up
exercises.biomechanics: Flexes the torso off the floor. Heavy activation of iliopsoas/rectus femoris (hip flexors) to lift the torso, causing spinal compression with minimal direct abdominal tension.
setup_cues: Lie flat on your back with knees bent and feet anchored.
Place hands behind head or crossed over chest.
Lift your entire torso off the floor until your chest touches your thighs.
Lower back down to the floor.
common_mistakes: Yanking the neck forward with hands.
Relying entirely on hip flexors instead of squeezing the abs.
Rounding and compressing the lumbar spine aggressively under load.
exercises.progression: Perform on a decline bench or hold a plate to your chest.
exercises.regression: Perform abdominal crunches (keeping lower back on the floor).

expert_rating.verdict: Low abdominal efficacy. Hip flexors perform the majority of the work while the lower back is heavily compressed.

exercises.plain_summary: Curl your torso up to your knees to work your hip flexors, though it can stress your lower back.

exercises.name: Abdominal Crunch
exercises.biomechanics: Isolates the upper rectus abdominis by flexing only the thoracic spine, keeping the lumbar spine flat on the floor.
setup_cues: Lie on back with knees bent, feet flat on the floor.
Place fingers lightly behind ears, keeping elbows wide.
Contract abs to lift shoulders off the floor while pressing lower back down.
Exhale and squeeze at the top, then slowly lower shoulders down.
common_mistakes: Pulling on the head/neck.
Lifting the lower back off the floor, which engages the hip flexors.
Using momentum to bounce off the floor.
exercises.progression: Decline crunch or cable crunch to add range and resistance.
exercises.regression: Hand-slide crunch (sliding hands up thighs toward knees).

expert_rating.verdict: Slightly better than sit-ups because it excludes hip flexors, but has a very limited range of motion.

exercises.plain_summary: Raise just your shoulders off the floor to isolate and squeeze the upper portion of your six-pack abs.

exercises.name: Ab Crunch Machine
exercises.biomechanics: Loads spinal flexion through a fixed machine path, letting the rectus abdominis work against adjustable resistance through a fuller range than a floor crunch.
setup_cues: Adjust the seat so the pad sits at mid-chest and the pivot aligns with your torso.
Grip the handles lightly — drive with the abs, not the arms.
Exhale and crunch the ribcage toward the pelvis.
Return slowly without letting the stack touch down between reps.
common_mistakes: Pulling with the arms instead of flexing the trunk.
Using a load so heavy the hips drive the movement.
Rushing the eccentric and letting the stack slam.
exercises.progression: Increase stack weight or add a 1-second squeeze at peak contraction.
exercises.regression: Lighter stack, or abdominal crunch on the floor.

expert_rating.verdict: Best crunch variation for progressive overload: machine stability plus adjustable load makes ab training trackable like any other lift.

exercises.plain_summary: Curl forward against weighted resistance on a machine to build your front abs through a controlled, guided path.

exercises.name: Hack Squat
exercises.biomechanics: Fixed linear travel removes lateral stability demands, allowing high loading. Placing feet lower on the platform increases knee flexion and quad stretch, while higher feet shift work to the glutes.
setup_cues: Position shoulders and back firmly against the pads.
Place feet shoulder-width apart on the platform, mid-to-low height.
Disengage safety handles, brace core, and lower under control until thighs are parallel to footplate.
Drive up through the mid-foot, avoiding knee lock at the top.
common_mistakes: Lifting heels off the platform at the bottom of the rep.
Allowing knees to cave inward (valgus collapse).
Lifting lower back or hips off the backrest.
exercises.progression: Increase plate loading or add a brief pause at the bottom stretch.
exercises.regression: Leg press or goblet box squat.

expert_rating.verdict: An absolute gold standard for quad hypertrophy. Extremely stable, allows safe training to failure, and provides a massive loaded stretch.

exercises.plain_summary: Squat on a guided sled machine to focus entirely on building your thighs without needing to balance a barbell.

exercises.name: Diverging Lat Pulldown Machine
exercises.biomechanics: The diverging path follows the natural motion of the shoulder blades, increasing the contraction sweep and aligning perfectly with the lat fibers.
setup_cues: Adjust seat height and knee pads so you are firmly locked in.
Grip handles unilaterally or bilaterally, chest up.
Pull shoulders down and back, driving elbows down toward your hips.
Control the path back up, allowing a full stretch at the top.
common_mistakes: Shrugging shoulders up at the bottom of the pull.
Leaning back excessively to use bodyweight.
Pulling with hands or biceps rather than leading with elbows.
exercises.progression: Increase machine weight while keeping strict form.
exercises.regression: Standard lat pulldown or assisted pull-up.

expert_rating.verdict: Outstanding unilateral lat builder. Highly stable seat lock with converging/diverging handle arcs that match lat anatomy better than a straight bar.

exercises.plain_summary: Pull down handles that spread outward to follow your shoulder blade motion, building wide back wings in a natural path.

exercises.name: Selectorized Bicep Curl Machine
exercises.biomechanics: Secures the upper arm on a pad, preventing shoulder flexion (cheating) and isolating elbow flexion. The cam design provides continuous tension.
setup_cues: Adjust seat height so your armpits rest comfortably at the top of the pad.
Align the elbow joint with the pivot axis of the machine.
Grip handles, keep chest tall, and curl handles toward shoulders.
Lower under control, extending elbows fully at the bottom.
common_mistakes: Lifting elbows off the pad during the curl.
Hunching shoulders forward or using torso momentum.
Stopping short of full extension.
exercises.progression: Increase weight stack or hold the peak contraction.
exercises.regression: Cable bicep curl or light dumbbell curl.

expert_rating.verdict: Extremely high stability isolates the elbow flexors perfectly. The machine cam curve maintains tension throughout the range of motion.

exercises.plain_summary: Curl padded machine levers upward to keep constant tension on your biceps and build the front of your arm.

exercises.name: Selectorized Triceps Extension Machine
exercises.biomechanics: A seated position with chest and elbow support isolates the triceps, providing a stabilized path for elbow extension.
setup_cues: Adjust seat so chest rests against the support pad.
Place elbows on the pad, aligning them with the machine's pivot point.
Extend arms fully, pushing the handles away.
Slowly return to the start position, controlling the eccentric stretch.
common_mistakes: Allowing elbows to flare outward off the pads.
Using chest/shoulder press mechanics instead of pure elbow extension.
Cutting the range of motion short.
exercises.progression: Increase weight stack or add a 1-second pause at full extension.
exercises.regression: Cable tricep pushdown.

expert_rating.verdict: High-stability setup that removes core/shoulder balance demands, making it excellent for safe, high-effort triceps isolation.

exercises.plain_summary: Push down padded levers on a seated machine to isolate and build the triceps on the back of your arms.

exercises.name: Assisted Chest Dip
exercises.biomechanics: Allows progressive overload of the chest dip by offloading bodyweight. Leaning forward targets lower pectoralis major fibers.
setup_cues: Set the assist weight stack (higher weight = easier).
Place knees or feet on the pad and grip handles, chest out.
Lean forward slightly (30 degrees) and lower until chest feels stretched.
Press back up, focusing on squeezing the chest, avoiding shoulder shrugging.
common_mistakes: Staying too upright, shifting focus entirely to triceps.
Allowing shoulders to roll forward (internal rotation) at the bottom.
Dropping too fast into the deep stretch position.
exercises.progression: Reduce the assist weight on the machine.
exercises.regression: Push-ups or chest press machine.

expert_rating.verdict: Excellent lower chest developer. The assist pad makes dips accessible and controllable, allowing safe training in the deep stretched range.

exercises.plain_summary: Lower and raise your body on bars with a helper platform to train your lower chest and triceps safely.

exercises.name: Kettlebell Swing
exercises.biomechanics: A dynamic, explosive hip hinge that trains rapid deceleration and acceleration of the posterior chain.
setup_cues: Stand with feet slightly wider than shoulder width, kettlebell 1 foot in front of you.
Hinge at the hips, keeping back flat, and grab kettlebell handle.
Hike kettlebell back between legs, then snap hips forward explosively.
Let kettlebell float to chest height; do not pull it up with arms.
common_mistakes: Squatting the weight up and down instead of hinging.
Using arms to lift the kettlebell.
Arching the lower back at the top.
exercises.progression: Increase kettlebell weight or swing single-arm.
exercises.regression: Dumbbell romanian deadlift or hip hinge practice.

expert_rating.verdict: Fantastic explosive power and posterior chain conditioning tool. Excellent for coordination, though barbell/dumbbell hinges are superior for pure mechanical tension hypertrophy.

exercises.plain_summary: Swing a kettlebell between your legs and up to chest height to build explosive hips, glutes, and thighs.

exercises.name: Captain's Chair Hanging Leg Raise
exercises.biomechanics: A supported forearm position stabilizes the upper body, allowing active hip flexion and posterior pelvic tilt to isolate the lower abs.
setup_cues: Rest forearms on the pads, gripping the handles firmly.
Press shoulders down away from ears, supporting bodyweight.
Raise legs (straight or bent knees) by curling the pelvis upward.
Lower legs slowly, resisting gravity, avoiding swinging.
common_mistakes: Swinging legs and using momentum.
Hanging passively with shoulders shrugged up to ears.
Lifting legs using hip flexors only, without tilting the pelvis to engage abs.
exercises.progression: Perform with straight legs or add a pause at the peak contraction.
exercises.regression: Hanging knee raise or dead bug.

expert_rating.verdict: Highly effective core builder. The captain's chair pads provide excellent upper body stability, preventing the swinging common in hanging bar leg raises.

exercises.plain_summary: Support your body on forearm pads and raise your legs to isolate and build your lower abs safely.

exercises.name: Cardio Stairmaster / Stepmill
exercises.biomechanics: An active climbing motion that forces unilateral leg extension under bodyweight load, building cardiovascular capacity and lower body muscular endurance.
setup_cues: Step onto the machine and select speed/level.
Keep posture upright, chest tall, avoiding leaning heavily on side handles.
Step through the full foot, pushing through the heel to engage glutes.
Maintain a steady, rhythmic breathing pace.
common_mistakes: Leaning far forward and supporting bodyweight with arms on the handrails.
Taking tiny, rapid steps instead of full strides.
Allowing knees to cave inward while stepping.
exercises.progression: Increase level (stepping speed) or session duration.
exercises.regression: Treadmill incline walking.

expert_rating.verdict: Top-tier cardio builder that also stimulates lower-body endurance. Excellent for active recovery and cardiovascular conditioning without joint impact stress.

exercises.plain_summary: Climb steps on a continuous machine to build cardiovascular fitness while strengthening your thighs, glutes, and lower legs.

exercises.name: Cardio Elliptical Trainer
exercises.biomechanics: Low-impact closed-loop elliptical path that provides smooth cardiovascular stimulus without ground impact, allowing active arm contribution.
setup_cues: Step onto footplates and grip handles.
Start pedaling in a forward motion.
Push and pull the handles rhythmically, keeping core engaged.
Maintain tall posture with hips and chest aligned forward.
common_mistakes: Standing on toes, causing foot numbness.
Allowing heels to lift excessively off the plates.
Leaning heavily on handles, reducing lower body effort.
exercises.progression: Increase resistance or incline level on console.
exercises.regression: Treadmill walking.

expert_rating.verdict: Great low-impact cardiovascular tool, particularly effective for joint-friendly active recovery and endurance workouts.

exercises.plain_summary: Glide in a smooth, low-impact stride to build your heart health and warm up your thighs and glutes.

exercises.name: Kneeling Hip Flexor (Couch Stretch)
exercises.biomechanics: By flexing the knee and extending the hip simultaneously, this places the rectus femoris and psoas under an intense, active stretch. Corrects anterior pelvic tilt and tight hips from prolonged sitting.
setup_cues: Kneel on a soft pad in front of a wall or a bench.
Place one knee close to the base of the wall, with your shin running straight up the wall.
Step the other foot forward into a lunge position, keeping your knee stacked over the ankle.
Slowly squeeze your glutes and bring your torso upright until you feel a deep stretch in the front of your hip.
common_mistakes: Arching the lower back excessively to make the torso upright, bypassing the hip stretch.
Allowing the front knee to cave inward.
Not actively squeezing the glute on the stretched side.
exercises.progression: Bring the knee closer to the wall and lift your chest higher.
exercises.regression: Perform a standard half-kneeling lunge stretch without the wall support.
exercises.plain_summary: Kneel with one foot raised against a wall to deeply stretch your hip flexors and the front of your thighs.

exercises.name: Wall Calf & Ankle Stretch
exercises.biomechanics: Loads the gastrocnemius and soleus under passive dorsiflexion, which directly improves ankle range of motion—the primary constraint in deep squatting mechanics.
setup_cues: Stand facing a wall, about one arm length away.
Place hands on the wall for support, and step one foot back.
Keep the back leg straight, heel flat on the floor, and front knee bent.
Lean forward slightly to increase the calf stretch, holding for time.
common_mistakes: Lifting the back heel off the floor.
Turning the back foot outward, which rotates the ankle out of alignment.
Arching the spine.
exercises.progression: Step the back foot further away from the wall.
exercises.regression: Perform seated with a resistance band looped around the foot.
exercises.plain_summary: Lean against a wall with your back heel down to stretch your calf muscles and improve your ankle mobility.

exercises.name: Cat-Cow Stretch
exercises.biomechanics: Promotes spinal flexion and extension, mobilizing the vertebrae and hydrating the intervertebral discs. Helps establish neuromuscular control of the pelvis (anterior/posterior tilt).
setup_cues: Start on all fours (tabletop position) with hands under shoulders and knees under hips.
Inhale, drop your belly toward the floor, lift your chest and chin, looking forward (Cow).
Exhale, round your spine toward the ceiling, tuck your chin to your chest, and pull your belly button in (Cat).
Flow smoothly between the two positions, matching breath to movement.
common_mistakes: Using jerky or rapid movements.
Hyperextending the neck in the cow position.
Forcing ranges of motion that cause pain.
exercises.progression: Add lateral movements or torso circles between transitions.
exercises.regression: Perform seated in a chair, rounding and arching the back.
exercises.plain_summary: Arch and round your back on your hands and knees to mobilize your spine and loosen stiff back muscles.

exercises.name: Lying Glute Stretch (Figure-Four)
exercises.biomechanics: Stretches the gluteal muscles and deep hip rotators (such as the piriformis) through hip flexion and external rotation, reducing sciatic nerve compression and lower back tightness.
setup_cues: Lie flat on your back with knees bent and feet flat on the floor.
Cross your right ankle over your left knee, creating a '4' shape.
Reach through your legs and grab the back of your left thigh or shin.
Gently pull your left knee toward your chest until you feel a stretch in your right outer hip/glute.
common_mistakes: Yanking the knee aggressively, straining the knee joint.
Lifting the lower back completely off the floor.
Tensing the head and shoulders instead of keeping them relaxed.
exercises.progression: Gently press the right knee outward with your elbow while pulling the left leg closer.
exercises.regression: Perform seated in a chair, crossing the leg and leaning forward.
exercises.plain_summary: Pull your crossed leg toward your chest while lying down to stretch your glutes and relieve hip tightness.

exercises.name: Foam Roller Thoracic Extension
exercises.biomechanics: Isolates extension of the thoracic spine (upper/mid back) over the fulcrum of the foam roller, reducing kyphosis and improving thoracic mobility necessary for overhead alignment.
setup_cues: Place the foam roller on the floor and lie back so it rests horizontally across your mid-back (lower shoulder blades).
Support your head with your hands, keeping elbows pointing forward.
Keep your hips on the floor, brace your core, and gently arch your upper back backward over the roller.
Inhale as you extend backward, then exhale and return to start. Roll up or down 1 inch and repeat.
common_mistakes: Flaring the lower ribs and arching the lower back (lumbar spine) instead of the upper back.
Letting your head drop back without hand support, straining the neck.
Rolling onto the lower back (which lacks ribs for protection).
exercises.progression: Extend arms overhead during the extension.
exercises.regression: Perform seated against a high-backed chair, arching backward gently.
exercises.plain_summary: Lie back over a foam roller to stretch your upper back and chest, reversing the slouched posture of daily sitting.

exercises.name: Hiking
exercises.biomechanics: Sustained loaded locomotion over grade. Ascents drive concentric quad/glute/calf work and aerobic demand; descents impose heavy eccentric quad loading and repetitive lateral-knee stress (IT band) that untrained legs adapt to slowly.
setup_cues: Shorten your stride and increase cadence on steep grades, up and down.
On descents, land soft with a bent knee and keep the pelvis level.
Use trekking poles on long descents to offload the knees.
Fuel and drink early on efforts over two hours.
common_mistakes: Braking down descents with long, straight-leg strides — this is what shreds knees and IT bands.
Going out at an unsustainable heart rate instead of a pace you can hold.
Skipping downhill/eccentric conditioning before a big mountain day.
exercises.plain_summary: Walking mountains. Uphill builds legs, lungs, and heart; downhill hammers the knees with eccentric (lowering) load — the part gym training rarely prepares you for.
exercises.progression: Longer or steeper hikes; add pack weight; faster ascent pace at a sustainable heart rate.
exercises.regression: Shorter, flatter hikes or incline treadmill walking.
